opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to having been forced, early on, to live in more than one world at once. In my own case, I started doing research very young, and I bounced between labs: some doing biochemistry, some doing neuroscience, some doing genome engineering. At first that felt disorienting, because every field has its own dialect, its own sense of what counts as a good experiment, its own taste. But over time you realize the underlying patterns rhyme. A problem in protein engineering looks a lot like a search problem in machine learning. A question about how cells keep state looks a lot like a question about memory in computation.

So part of it is exposure, but exposure alone isn't enough. You have to actually go deep enough in each area that you can do the work with your own hands. You can't just read the abstracts. The generalization only comes when you've internalized the constraints of a system, what's cheap, what's expensive, what's measurable, what's noise. Then when you see something surprising in one domain, you have a mental library of analogous structures to map it onto.

The other piece is temperament. You need to be comfortable being a beginner over and over again, and kind of shameless about asking naive questions. Some of the most useful ideas come from someone saying, "Wait, why do you do it that way?" and the honest answer being, "Historical accident." Fields accumulate a lot of path dependence, and outsiders are often the ones who notice it.

And then I'd say environment matters enormously. Institutions tend to reward depth within a silo: your grants, your papers, your tenure case. So if you want people to generalize across boundaries, you have to build places where it's normal to have a computational person, a wet lab biologist, and an engineer sitting at the same bench, arguing about the same problem. That's a big part of why we set up Arc the way we did. Cross-disciplinary insight isn't a mystical gift; it's something you can cultivate if you design the incentives and the physical and intellectual proximity right.

r001.rationale: The response describes mapping analogous patterns between fields, but does not characterize this as out-of-distribution generalization.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes hands-on experience across fields and says reading abstracts alone is insufficient; it does not identify reading across disciplines as a foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to being forced to take an observation in one context and ask whether it's actually a general principle or just a local quirk of the system you happen to be looking at. When I was coming up, the training was really about depth in one area, and I think that's necessary, you need to know at least one thing deeply enough to recognize what a real result looks like versus noise. But the generalization part is a different muscle. It usually comes from exposure, from sitting in rooms with people who speak a completely different scientific language and realizing that the thing they're describing is structurally the same problem you've been working on.

In my own case, a lot of the way I think about biology got shaped by hanging out with people doing computation and engineering. Biologists tend to think in terms of mechanism and specific molecules. Engineers think in terms of systems and abstractions and what the interfaces are. Once you start toggling between those modes, you start seeing CRISPR not just as a bacterial immune system but as a programmable search function, or seeing a genome less as a static parts list and more as something closer to a language with syntax you could learn. Those reframings only happen if you've absorbed enough of the other field's mental models that you can run them on your own data.

The other piece is that good scientists tend to be a little bit obsessive about anomalies. When something doesn't fit, most people explain it away. The people who end up generalizing across fields are the ones who hold onto the weird result and keep carrying it around until they encounter a framework somewhere else that suddenly makes it make sense. So I'd say it's a combination of real depth somewhere, broad curiosity, a tolerance for feeling like a beginner over and over again, and a willingness to be the person in the room asking the naive question. Honestly the naive question is where most of the cross-disciplinary insight comes from, because the expert has usually stopped asking it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses distinguishing general principles from local quirks and applying other fields’ mental models, but does not characterize this as out-of-distribution generalization.

r002.rationale: It credits exposure to people and ideas from other fields, but does not identify reading across scientific disciplines as a foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes from spending time being a beginner in more than one field. You learn that what one discipline treats as an obvious assumption, another discipline might treat as an open question. That gives you a chance to distinguish the underlying phenomenon from the particular language people use to describe it.

But you also need depth. It’s easy to draw an analogy between biology and computing; it’s much harder to figure out where that analogy makes a useful prediction and where it breaks down. So I think the ability develops through a cycle: you encounter something surprising, connect it to an idea from elsewhere, and then test whether that connection actually explains anything.

Talking to people who think differently is a big part of that. When you have to explain an observation to someone who doesn’t share your assumptions, you often discover which parts you understand and which parts you’ve just learned to repeat.

r001.rationale: The response describes connecting surprising observations to ideas from other fields and testing the connection, but does not characterize this as out-of-distribution generalization.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning across fields and talking with people who think differently, but does not identify reading across scientific disciplines as a foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from spending time in situations where you’re a beginner again. Within a field, you learn which questions people consider important, what counts as evidence, and which assumptions you can take for granted. When you move into another discipline, those assumptions become visible. You start asking, “Is this a fundamental constraint, or is this just how we’ve learned to approach the problem?”

But making a connection is only the beginning. You need enough depth to understand where an analogy breaks down, and you need people from that other field who can challenge you. Otherwise, it’s easy to mistake a shared vocabulary for a shared mechanism.

So I think that ability develops through a cycle of curiosity, immersion, and testing. You encounter something surprising, build a mental model that might explain it, and then ask whether that model makes a useful prediction somewhere else. The feedback from that prediction is what helps you learn which ideas actually travel across boundaries.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning across fields through curiosity, immersion, and testing, but does not characterize it as out-of-distribution generalization.

r002.rationale: It discusses moving into another discipline and learning from people there, but does not identify reading across disciplines as a foundation.
